title: A 95-Year-Old Man Remembers the Girl He Lost to Partition. Imtiaz Ali Built a Whole Film Around That Memory.
excerpt: Main Vaapas Aaunga pairs Vedang Raina and Sharvari as doomed young lovers, Naseeruddin Shah as the man who never forgot, and Diljit Dosanjh as the grandson who crosses borders to keep a promise. A.R. Rahman's score ties it all together.
body:
There is a moment early in **Main Vaapas Aaunga** where **Diljit Dosanjh**'s character Nirvair pauses over something that doesn't quite add up. His 95-year-old grandfather Keenu — played by **Naseeruddin Shah** with the kind of translucent frailty that makes you hold your breath — can remember every detail about a girl he met 78 years ago in undivided India. Her laugh. The way she tied her dupatta. The exact tree they sat under. But he can't remember what he had for lunch.

<youtube></youtube>

It's a small observation, but it cracks open the entire film. **Imtiaz Ali** has always been interested in the way love rewires memory, how certain people become permanent architecture inside us. With Main Vaapas Aaunga, releasing in theaters today, he's finally gone to the place he's been circling for years: 1947 and the wound that split a subcontinent and severed millions of love stories that history never bothered to record.

The film unfolds across two timelines. In the first, young Keenu — played by **Vedang Raina** with a looseness and charm that suggest a star settling into his range — falls for Jiya, a Muslim girl played by **Sharvari**. Their love is the Ali signature: impulsive, sun-drenched, built on stolen glances and whispered certainties. They know the world around them is fracturing. They make promises anyway.

> "If I had a choice between death and leaving my home, I would have gladly chosen death. Unfortunately, I did not have such a choice." — Anonymous refugee, featured in the film's special video *Kya Kamaal Hai*

In the second timeline, Keenu is 95 and running out of time. His body is failing but that one memory won't leave. An unfulfilled promise to Jiya — one the audience pieces together slowly — is keeping him tethered to a world he no longer fully inhabits. Enter Nirvair, his grandson, a modern Sikh man who crosses the border to Pakistan to close a loop that has been open for nearly eight decades.

The casting is, frankly, inspired. Raina and Sharvari bring an innocence to their scenes that never feels performed — their chemistry is the kind that makes you forget you're watching two actors who've probably rehearsed this fifty times. Shah does what Shah does: makes you feel like you're watching a real human being decompose before your eyes, one memory at a time. And Dosanjh — who could have coasted on charisma — grounds Nirvair in a quiet, searching earnestness that provides the emotional spine of the entire second half.

The first half, admittedly, takes its time. Imtiaz Ali has never been a filmmaker in a hurry, and here the pacing occasionally tests your patience. The period setting is lush — the production design and **A.R. Rahman**'s score create a world that feels tactile and alive — but the narrative engine idles too long in the setup. You know where the story is going. You're waiting for it to get there.

When it does, though, it lands. The second half tightens into something genuinely moving. Nirvair's journey across the border becomes a meditation on what we owe the people who came before us, and the closure he delivers to his grandfather is handled with a tenderness that only Ali at his best can manage. It's the kind of filmmaking that earns its tears rather than manufacturing them.

Early reviews are mixed — critics have noted the slow burn — but the consensus seems to be that when Main Vaapas Aaunga works, it *works*. **Kabir Khan** and **Sunidhi Chauhan** were among the industry voices praising the film after a special screening, with Chauhan calling the music "incredible."

For NRI audiences, this is essential viewing. Partition stories carry a different weight in the diaspora, where the aftershocks of 1947 still echo in family histories, in the neighborhoods our grandparents describe, in the borders that separate us from people who share our blood. Ali, working with lyricist **Irshad Kamil** and Rahman, has crafted a film that speaks directly to that inheritance.

Main Vaapas Aaunga releases today, June 12, in theaters worldwide. It opens against a crowded field — **Governor**, **Bharat Bhagya Vidhata**, and **Haunted 3D** are all hitting screens the same day — but Ali's name and that cast should give it legs in multiplexes. Trade estimates suggest it needs ₹5-7 crore on opening day to maintain healthy numbers against a ₹70 crore budget.

Go see it on the big screen. Rahman's score deserves a theater sound system, and Naseeruddin Shah's face deserves to be thirty feet tall.
